I still have the drive to do them, but I just keep getting sidetracked and forgetting what I need.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any difficulties with language, such as finding the right words or following conversations, in addition to your memory and focus issues?\n\nPatient: I don't have any trouble finding the right words. My struggles are purely about staying focused, keeping track of details, and remembering to do things.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you've experienced any episodes of sudden, brief periods of confusion or disorientation, which might help differentiate between potential cognitive issues?\n\nPatient: No, I have never experienced any sudden periods of confusion or disorientation. Once my days became more unstructured, I found it increasingly difficult to keep track of all my responsibilities.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any difficulties with learning new information, following instructions, or making decisions, in addition to the memory problems you've described?\n\nPatient: Yes, I really struggle with following through; I'll start planning a church event but get distracted by laundry or a phone call and leave it half-done. I also find my mind drifting when trying to read committee notes or follow a Bible study, so I miss a lot of that new information. Making decisions is fine, but staying focused to finish what I start is where I have trouble.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how you feel about your husband's passing and your retirement, and if you've been having any thoughts or feelings that might be contributing to your difficulties with focus and memory?\n\nPatient: While losing my husband and retiring were huge adjustments, I don't feel depressed or overwhelmed by grief. The real issue is that those changes left me with a completely unstructured schedule, and I ended up taking on too many volunteer projects to fill my time. Without a set daily routine, it has become incredibly difficult to keep track of everything, which is why I'm struggling so much with my focus.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any times or situations where your memory and focus seem to be better, such as when you're doing something you enjoy or when you have a very structured schedule?\n\nPatient: Yes, definitely. When I was working as a senior center coordinator, having a structured schedule helped me stay much more organized and reliable. Now, even with activities I truly enjoy like gardening or quilting, I still find my mind drifting off and getting distracted because my days are so unstructured.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant loss of interest in activities that you used to enjoy, such as gardening or quilting, or has your lack of focus been the main issue?\n\nPatient: Oh, I haven't lost interest at all; I still very much want to stay active with my gardening and quilting. The main issue is definitely my lack of focus and getting distracted, which makes it hard to follow through on these projects. I still have the drive to do them, but I just keep getting sidetracked and forgetting what I need.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any difficulties with language, such as finding the right words or following conversations, in addition to your memory and focus issues?\n\nPatient: I don't have any trouble finding the right words. But I definitely struggle to follow conversations because my mind will drift off after a few minutes, and I'll realize I've missed half of what the other person was saying.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe any difficulties you've experienced with performing daily tasks that require planning or problem-solving, such as managing your finances or preparing meals?\n\nPatient: I haven't really had much trouble with managing my finances or cooking meals specifically. However, I do tend to get very sidetracked when I'm trying to plan or organize other things, like my volunteer projects or church events.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that your memory and focus issues started after significant life changes, but you don't feel depressed or overwhelmed by grief. Can you tell me if you've experienced any periods of persistent sadness or loss of pleasure in activities that you normally enjoy, even if it's not a major issue for you now?\n\nPatient: No, I really haven't experienced any persistent sadness or lost pleasure in the things I love to do. My main struggle has just been the deep frustration of trying to keep up with all my commitments and feeling like I'm constantly falling short. I still want to do everything, I just can't seem to stay on top of it all.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you've noticed any difficulties with recalling recent events, learning new skills, or recognizing familiar people or places, which might help clarify what's going on with your memory and focus?\n\nPatient: No, I don't have any trouble recognizing familiar people or places, learning new skills, or recalling past events. My forgetfulness is strictly about keeping track of my daily routines and tasks, like remembering to take my pills or bringing what I need to my meetings. It's not that I'm losing my memory of the past or getting disoriented; I just can't seem to keep my day-to-day schedule straight.\n\nDoctor: Can you rate your overall motivation to participate in daily activities and social events, despite your struggles with focus and memory, to help me understand if there's an underlying issue with motivation or if it's purely a cognitive challenge?\n\nPatient: My motivation is actually very high, and I'm constantly on the go, bouncing from one volunteer project, church activity, or family task to the next. I genuinely want to do all of these things and have a hard time just sitting still, so it's not a lack of motivation at all. It is purely a struggle with keeping track of everything, staying focused, and organizing my unstructured time.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situations where you feel completely focused and able to remember everything you need to, without any distractions or memory lapses, and if so, what's different about those situations compared to your daily struggles?\n\nPatient: I honestly can't think of any situations lately where I feel completely focused or free from these memory lapses. These struggles seem to spill into almost everything I try to do nowadays, leaving me feeling constantly scattered. I just can't seem to find any \"zone\" of perfect focus anymore, no matter what I'm doing.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any times when you've felt a strong sense of purpose or engagement in an activity, and if so, did your memory and focus improve during those times?\n\nPatient: Even when I am deeply passionate and engaged in my volunteer work or church projects, I still seem to struggle with these memory lapses and focus issues. I'm not entirely sure if my focus gets any better just because I feel a strong sense of purpose. It seems like the forgetfulness and drifting mind happen regardless of how much the project means to me.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any difficulties with self-monitoring, such as checking your work for errors or keeping track of your progress on tasks, which might be related to your struggles with focus and memory?\n\nPatient: Yes, I really struggle with that; when filling out volunteer paperwork, I'll skim through and think I've done it perfectly, only for someone to point out I skipped whole sections or wrote the wrong dates. I also can't seem to track my progress because I'll start planning a church outreach, get distracted by chores or a phone call, and just wander off without finishing.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if you've experienced any decline in your ability to perform tasks that require complex thinking, problem-solving, or judgment, compared to your past abilities?\n\nPatient: I haven't really noticed any decline in my actual ability to think deeply, solve problems, or make decisions. My struggles are purely about staying focused, keeping track of details, and remembering to do things.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you've experienced any episodes of sudden, brief periods of confusion or disorientation, which might help differentiate between potential cognitive issues?\n\nPatient: No, I have never experienced any sudden periods of confusion or disorientation. My difficulties are strictly about forgetting my tasks, getting distracted, or losing track of what I'm supposed to do, rather than feeling confused about where I am.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any difficulties with word-finding, understanding written or spoken language, or with motor functions such as walking or using your hands, which could help clarify the nature of your cognitive issues?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't experienced any of those difficulties; I don't have trouble finding words, understanding language, or with physical skills like walking or using my hands. The only things I notice are that I tend to fidget a lot when I'm sitting, and sometimes my mind drifts so I lose track of what people are saying. Otherwise, my physical and basic language abilities are completely fine.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned feeling jittery when you have to sit still and that you tend to fidget a lot; can you tell me more about how often this happens and if it's interfering with your daily activities?\n\nPatient: It happens quite often, especially when I have to sit still for a long time, like during church sermons or council meetings. I constantly tap my foot, fiddle with my keys, or rearrange papers because of a pent-up, jittery feeling inside that makes me feel like I just have to get up and move. This restlessness makes it incredibly hard for me to pay attention and stay present during these important activities.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how often you experience this jittery feeling and fidgeting, and if it's always present or if there are specific times or situations when it's more pronounced?\n\nPatient: It’s not always present, but it becomes much more pronounced when I am forced to sit still for a long time, like during a long church sermon or a council meeting. In those situations, I get this pent-up, jittery sensation inside that makes me feel like I just have to get up and move. To cope with that feeling, I find myself constantly tapping my foot, fiddling with my keys, or rearranging the papers in front of me.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever been diagnosed with or experienced symptoms of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) in the past, and if so, how have those symptoms impacted your daily life?\n\nPatient: I have never been formally diagnosed, but looking back, I definitely struggled with these symptoms as a child; my grade school report cards often said I daydreamed too much, forgot my homework, and talked out of turn. These issues have really started getting in the way over the last two years since my husband passed and I retired, to the point where people at church have stopped relying on me for important tasks. Even my daughter has started double-checking my plans because she worries I'll drop the ball with my grandkids' schedules.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have difficulty sustaining focus during tasks that you find enjoyable or interesting, or if your mind tends to wander only during tasks that you find boring or unengaging?\n\nPatient: Yes, this difficulty happens even with tasks I genuinely care about and enjoy, like reading my garden committee notes, preparing for church outreach, or following a Bible study. My mind will still drift off or I'll get distracted and wander away to do other things, even when I really want to stay focused on these meaningful projects."

In those situations, I get this pent-up, jittery sensation inside that makes me feel like I just have to get up and move. These issues have really started getting in the way over the last two years since my husband passed and I retired, to the point where people at church have stopped relying on me for important tasks.
